{
  "approach": "Model this as a finite-source (machine-repairman) M/M/c//10 queue: 10 sources (robots), each idle source generates requests at rate 0.5/hr only when not in service, service is exponential mean 1 hr (rate 1 per technician), c technicians with no waiting (blocked if all c busy). Find smallest c such that blocking probability = probability all c technicians busy = Erlang-B-like formula for finite population: B = [C(10,c) * (0.5/1)^c] / [sum_{k=0}^c C(10,k) * (0.5/1)^k]. Compute for c=1,2,3,... until B < 0.05. Verify by evaluating the exact formula.",
  "steps": [
    "Define arrival intensity per idle robot: lambda = 0.5 requests/hour; service rate per technician: mu = 1 per hour; number of sources N = 10; offered load per source rho = lambda/mu = 0.5.",
    "Recognize this is an M/M/c//N finite-population loss system (blocked customers are lost; there is no queue).",
    "State the exact blocking probability for finite sources: B(c) = C(N,c) * rho^c / sum_{k=0}^c C(N,k) * rho^k, where C(N,k) is binomial coefficient.",
    "Evaluate B(c) incrementally: c=1: B=(10*0.5)/(1+10*0.5)=5/6≈0.8333. c=2: B=[45*0.25]/[1+5+11.25]=11.25/17.25≈0.6522. c=3: B=[120*0.125]/[1+5+11.25+15]=15/32.25≈0.4651. c=4: B=[210*0.0625]/[1+5+11.25+15+13.125]=13.125/45.375≈0.2893. c=5: B=[252*0.03125]/[1+5+11.25+15+13.125+7.875]=7.875/53.25≈0.1479. c=6: B=[210*0.015625]/[1+5+11.25+15+13.125+7.875+3.28125]=3.28125/56.53125≈0.0580. c=7: B=[120*0.0078125]/[1+5+11.25+15+13.125+7.875+3.28125+0.9375]=0.9375/57.46875≈0.01631.",
    "Determine the smallest c with B(c) < 0.05: c=7 gives 1.63% < 5%, while c=6 gives 5.80% > 5%; therefore c=7.",
    "Cross-check using the complement relation: for finite-source M/M/c//N with loss, B(c) = (P(all c busy)) from the truncated binomial state distribution, which matches the formula used.",
    "Conclude: 7 technicians are required, and despite the finite population, the blocking is driven by the high offered load (10 robots * 0.5 = 5 Erlangs) and randomness, so the infinite-source approximation (Erlang-B with 5 Erlangs) would also suggest 7 but it must not be used as the basis; the finite-source formula is the correct accounting.",
    "State final answer: smallest technician count = 7."
  ],
  "critical_invariants": [
    "Arrival rate applies only to idle robots: lambda = 0.5/hr per idle robot, so total offered load is not independent of c; it depends on how many robots are idle.",
    "Blocking probability is exactly the probability that all c technicians are busy in steady state, because blocked requests are lost and cannot wait.",
    "The finite-source state distribution is binomial truncated at c: P(k busy) proportional to C(N,k) * (lambda/mu)^k.",
    "Smallest c must be checked monotonically: find first c where B(c) < 0.05 (B decreases as c increases in this loss system).",
    "Do not use infinite-source Poisson arrivals (Erlang-B with rate 5/hr) as the sole justification; the advisory case, if supplied, must be validated against the finite-population formula.",
    "Service time mean is exactly 1 hour, so service rate mu = 1 per technician per hour."
  ],
  "assumptions": [
    "Each robot makes independent requests only while idle; requests while already in session do not occur.",
    "Technician service times are independent and exponentially distributed with mean 1 hour.",
    "Inter-arrival times for each idle robot are independent and exponentially distributed with rate 0.5/hour (Poisson process per idle robot).",
    "If all technicians are busy, a request is immediately blocked and lost, and the robot remains idle (retrying later is modeled by the idle-source Poisson process).",
    "The system reaches steady state and blocking probability is the long-run fraction of requests blocked.",
    "Technicians are identical; no priorities, preemption, or balking beyond blocking.",
    "The target asks for the smallest integer technician count satisfying the <5% blocking requirement."
  ]
}
